opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions, and it's really at the heart of how we've been thinking about memory in these architectures.

The way I like to frame it is that every component in a model is a kind of memory, and what distinguishes them is how often they update. If you look at a standard Transformer, you basically have two extremes. Attention updates at every token: it takes in the current context and immediately adapts to it. But once the context is gone, that information is gone. So it's very expressive, but it's short-term. On the other end, the MLP layers, the feed-forward weights, only get updated during pre-training. After that they're frozen. So they hold long-term knowledge, but they can't absorb anything new at test time.

What's missing is everything in between. In the brain, you don't just have these two extremes. You have a spectrum of processes operating at different timescales, different brain-wave frequencies if you want an analogy, and memory consolidation happens gradually as information moves from fast-changing systems to more stable ones.

So the intuition is this: a component that updates very frequently is great at adapting and capturing fine-grained, local information, but it's also more vulnerable to overwriting. New inputs keep pushing it around, so older information gets erased. A component that updates rarely is much more stable. It effectively compresses over a longer window, so it retains more persistent abstractions, but it's slower to adapt. There's a trade-off between plasticity and stability, and update frequency is basically the knob that controls it.

That's why we've been arguing for what we call a continuum of memory. Instead of one short-term memory and one long-term memory, you have a chain of memory modules, each updated at its own frequency. The fast ones handle what's happening right now. The slower ones gradually absorb what's consistently useful. And importantly, if something gets forgotten in a faster level, it can still survive in a slower level, and in some cases it can even be brought back. That helps a lot with catastrophic forgetting, which is a big problem when you want models that keep learning after deployment.

So my short answer is that update frequency largely determines what kind of memory a component can be. If you want a model that can actually learn continually, you can't just have the two extremes we have today. You need that whole spectrum in between.

r001.rationale: The candidate says components that update rarely are more stable and retain persistent abstractions over a longer window.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that I think update frequency is one of the most underappreciated knobs in how a model organizes memory, and it's really the core idea behind what we called nested learning.

If you think about the human brain, you don't have a single memory system. You have things that update extremely fast, like working memory, where information lives for seconds. Then there's short-term memory that persists over hours, and long-term memory that consolidates over days or years, and some of that is essentially fixed. Those systems operate at very different timescales, and the timescale is not an accident. It's what gives each system its role.

Now map that onto a neural network. In a standard Transformer, you effectively have two extremes. You have attention, which is updated every single token, so it's an extremely high-frequency, in-context memory. And you have the weights, which were updated during pretraining and then frozen, so their frequency at deployment is zero. There's nothing in between. That's the gap that causes a lot of what people call the continual learning problem. The model either memorizes something instantly and forgets it as soon as the context window ends, or it needs a full training run to absorb anything permanently.

So the way I think about it, every component of the model is itself a kind of associative memory, and it has a natural update frequency. The faster a component updates, the more it's dominated by recent information. It can capture very specific, surprising things about the immediate input, but it also gets overwritten quickly. It's high-plasticity, low-stability. The slower a component updates, the more it averages over long stretches of data. It captures abstractions and general structure, and it's robust, but it can't pick up anything new quickly. Retention and adaptability are in tension, and frequency is how you choose where on that tradeoff a given piece of the model sits.

What becomes interesting is when you stack several of these at different frequencies, nested inside each other. Think of it as a continuum memory system rather than a single memory. One level updates every token, the next one maybe every chunk of tokens, the next one every so many chunks, and so on, with the outermost level being close to the original pretrained weights. Each level compresses the information flowing through the faster level below it. So a fact that shows up once gets held briefly in the fast memory. If it keeps showing up, or if it generates a lot of surprise, it gets pushed into slower and slower levels, and that's what consolidation looks like inside the architecture.

And one thing I'd emphasize is that this isn't just about the memory module in isolation. Even the optimizer is an associative memory in this view. Momentum is a memory of past gradients, and its decay rate sets its effective frequency. So when we say nested learning, we mean the whole stack, from the attention state up through the training algorithm, is a set of nested optimization problems, each with its own clock. Once you see it that way, designing for better retention is really a question of choosing the right set of frequencies and deciding how information flows between them.

r001.rationale: The response says slower-updating components average over longer stretches and are more robust, while faster-updating components are overwritten quickly, communicating that less frequent updates support longer retention.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the frequency of updates determines the timescale of the memory. If a component updates very frequently, it can adapt quickly to new information, but its existing memories are also more exposed to being overwritten. If it updates less frequently, it changes more slowly, so it can preserve information over longer periods, but it’s less responsive to new experiences.

So there’s a tradeoff between plasticity and stability. And rather than choosing one update frequency for the entire model, you can have components operating at different frequencies. The faster components capture what’s happening right now, while the slower components retain more persistent knowledge. Update frequency alone doesn’t guarantee retention—the update rule matters too—but it gives you a way to organize memory across different timescales.

r001.rationale: The response says less frequent updates let a component change more slowly and preserve information over longer periods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think update frequency gives you a useful way to think about the timescale of memory. A component that updates very frequently can adapt quickly to new information, but its state is also more easily overwritten. A component that updates less frequently changes more slowly, so it can preserve information over longer periods, although it’s less responsive to what just happened.

The interesting design is to combine those timescales. You have fast components capturing the immediate context, and slower components retaining more persistent knowledge. Then the question becomes: what information is important enough to move from the fast-changing state into the slower-changing state? Updating slowly alone doesn’t give you useful memory; you also need a good mechanism for deciding what to retain.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a less frequently updated component changes more slowly and can preserve information over longer periods.
